{"id": "6:128/q32", "question": "Why end with 'Wise, Knowing'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q32/p1", "position": "God assigns recompense wisely and knows all deeds, states and deserts.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Zajjaj, Nahhas, Kashshaf, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi, Alusi and Elmalili explain the closing names through just measure of punishment and all-encompassing knowledge. Tabarsi allows specific knowledge of who merits reward or punishment. Qashani applies wisdom to acquired soul traits and temporary or endless punishment. Tabatabai says it explains the verdict to Muhammad."}, {"id": "6:128/q32/p2", "position": "The names explain divine foreknowledge of who will later believe and be excepted.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Baghawi cite decreed repentance, truthful faith and piety of heart; Ibn Atiyya makes the ending evidence for a present warning that excludes future believers."}, {"id": "6:128/q32/p3", "position": "The divine name emphasizes majesty in a judgment beyond objection.", "reasons": "Biqai says the greatest name manifests majesty and guards the divine station."}]}
{"id": "6:128/q33", "question": "How does this scene connect with nearby verses and the sūra?", "turns_on": "Different contextual emphases.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q33/p1", "position": "It develops jinn and human leader-follower exchanges elsewhere.", "reasons": "Biqai compares later blame among followers at 7:38 and the weak followers' admission at 7:75; Ibn Kathir links Satan's many followers to 36:60–62. Qurtubi and Baghawi compare the exception in 11:106–107."}, {"id": "6:128/q33/p2", "position": "It contrasts the promised Garden for guided people with warning of the Fire.", "reasons": "Razi describes promise followed by threat; Kuranyolu similarly moves from guided believers' Paradise to disbelievers' gathering. Biqai says the gathering day is a central theme veiled at the sūra's opening and disclosed in later passages."}, {"id": "6:128/q33/p3", "position": "It explains how wrongdoers become guardians of one another without injustice.", "reasons": "Tabatabai relates it to earlier verses and stresses their free response to warning; Islahi links the wrongdoers and tempters of 6:123–124."}, {"id": "6:128/q33/p4", "position": "It warns humans against the jinn's enticing of evil, since both groups are paired in Fire.", "reasons": "Wahidi cites the people of meaning; Kuranyolu describes a lasting voluntary alliance across generations."}]}
{"id": "6:128/q34", "question": "What is Qashani's inward reading of the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q34/p1", "position": "The jinn are lower-self powers that master senses, limbs or human forms and receive punishment matching acquired traits.", "reasons": "Qashani places the absolute unitive gathering against psychic powers and their bodily instruments. {"id": "6:128/q35", "question": "What separate reports illuminate the judgment, mercy, and intercession scene?", "turns_on": "Different reported events and their scope.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q35/p1", "position": "Repeated intercession releases believers from Hell; those bound by the Qur'an remain.", "reasons": "Anas's reports in Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, Bukhari, Ibn Majah and Muslim include God-set limits and faith as small as an atom or grain; Qatada identifies those eternally detained and connects the praised station to 17:79. Ibn Masud describes mercy after a divinely willed stay."}, {"id": "6:128/q35/p2", "position": "People follow their worshiped objects, cross Hell's bridge, and some believers are rescued.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra's accounts in Ahmad, Bukhari and Muslim describe the last entrant to Paradise; Abu Sa'id corrects the final gift to ten times the reported reward. One Ahmad report mentions 45:28."}, {"id": "6:128/q35/p3", "position": "Muhammad reserves his answered supplication for intercession on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Ahmad, Bukhari and Muslim transmit versions through Abu Hurayra; Ka'b asks whether he heard it directly, and Abu Hurayra confirms."}, {"id": "6:128/q35/p4", "position": "Believers are privately reckoned and forgiven, while unbelievers and hypocrites are exposed.", "reasons": "Ibn Hibban and Ibn Majah report this distinction with reference to 11:18."}, {"id": "6:128/q35/p5", "position": "A prophetic dream details punishments for neglecting Qur'an and prayer, lying, adultery and usury, and depicts children born on fitra and possible pardon for mixed deeds.", "reasons": "Ibn Hibban and Bukhari report Samura's dream; the children include those of polytheists."}, {"id": "6:128/q35/p6", "position": "Hell asks for more until filled, while Paradise receives new creation.", "reasons": "Abu Sa'id transmits this account twice in Ahmad, saying Paradise remains as long as God wills."}, {"id": "6:128/q35/p7", "position": "A believer who meets God affirming both testimonies is shielded from Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn Hibban relates the saying after an army's food multiplies."}, {"id": "6:128/q35/p8", "position": "The Prophet warned women about Hell, urged charity, and explained menstruation and testimony rules.", "reasons": "Ahmad reports Abu Hurayra's narration involving Zaynab and Ibn Masud's family."}, {"id": "6:128/q35/p9", "position": "The Prophet contrasted the Muslim's lesser eating with the unbeliever's seven intestines.", "reasons": "Ibn Hisham reports the saying after Thumama accepted Islam; the report also describes his capture, kind treatment, release and pledge."}, {"id": "6:128/q35/p10", "position": "Worldly poverty may accompany a Hereafter granted to believers.", "reasons": "Ibn Majah reports Umar's recollection of the Prophet's contrast with Persian and Byzantine rulers."}]}
{"id": "6:128/q36", "question": "What ancillary linguistic, historical, and recitation material is preserved with these notes?", "turns_on": "The distinct ancillary reports concern Arabic forms, Meccan history, prophetic biography, and recitation practice.", "positions": [{"id": "6:128/q36/p1", "position": "Ishmael's descendants and Jurhum successively held the Kaaba, while conflicts named Meccan sites.", "reasons": "Ibn Hisham gives Nabit then Mudad; Azraqi gives Ishmael's marriages, twelve sons, 130-year life, burial, Jurhum and Qatura settlement, kingship, fighting and site names Qayqaʿan, Ajyad, Fadih and al-Matabikh. Umar warns that profaning the sanctuary loses custody."}, {"id": "6:128/q36/p2", "position": "Arabic can preserve an original vowel pattern in lightened forms.", "reasons": "Sibawayh discusses shahida/laʿiba, niʿma/biʾsa, and ghuzī, citing al-Akhtal's line; these notes offer linguistic analogy without a direct gloss of a 6:128 word."}, {"id": "6:128/q36/p3", "position": "Hagar found Zamzam and Abraham with Ishmael built the House; later Jurhum lost it and Abd al-Muttalib rediscovered the well.", "reasons": "Azraqi reports Hagar's search as the origin of saʿy, Gabriel's opening of Zamzam, Jurhum settlement, Abraham's visits and the Maqam, varied accounts of the sakina, Jurhum's profanation, Khuzaʿa's conquest, and Zamzam's concealment and recovery."}, {"id": "6:128/q36/p4", "position": "Salman's route to Medina and accounts of prophetic signs and miracles are narrated.", "reasons": "Ibn Hisham recounts Salman's enslavement and recognition of Medina, pre-revelation greetings from stones and trees, Muhammad and Ali's prayer with Abu Talib's response, the trench rock, and the Tabuk spring."}, {"id": "6:128/q36/p5", "position": "Correct recitation depends on oral training and natural performance, with examples of distinguished reciters.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari reports conversions after Sibt al-Khayyat's recitation, names Badr al-Din and Ibrahim al-Hakari, cites al-Dani on practice, objects to affected mouth and voice manipulation, and laments a decline in the highest mastery."}, {"id": "6:128/q36/p6", "position": "A hidden spiritual realization about the exception is reserved for experienced wayfarers.", "reasons": "Bursevi attributes this advice to Najm al-Din, without specifying its content; the source also prays for a sound-hearted end."}, {"id": "6:128/q36/p7", "position": "A Persian admonition says to wake before death ends the opportunity to act.", "reasons": "Bursevi quotes verses about a sleeper who did no work before time passed."}]}

{"id": "6:146/q02", "question": "How is ظُفُرٍ read?", "turns_on": "Vowels on the ẓāʾ and fāʾ; some readers and transmitters vary.", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q02/p1", "position": "The fāʾ is still, with ḍamma on ẓāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿraj, al-Aʿmash, Ubayy and others are reported; Samīn calls it easing the ḍamma."}, {"id": "6:146/q02/p2", "position": "The ẓāʾ has kasra and the fāʾ is still.", "reasons": "Attributed variously to al-Ḥasan and Abū al-Sammāl; Abū Ḥātim rejects it, whereas al-Qurṭubī calls it a dialect."}, {"id": "6:146/q02/p3", "position": "Both consonants have kasra.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and Samīn attribute it to Abū al-Sammāl, Jishumī to Ibn al-Sammāl, Ālūsī to Abū al-Sammāk; the attributions vary."}, {"id": "6:146/q02/p4", "position": "The common reading has ḍamma on both ẓāʾ and fāʾ.", "reasons": "Jishumī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Samīn call it the majority or highest form; all forms are dialectal in Jishumī."}]}
{"id": "6:146/q03", "question": "What does ظُفُرٍ mean as a word?", "turns_on": "Whether hoof is a literal or figurative extension of nail.", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q03/p1", "position": "It is a nail, claw or terminal digit; its forms and plurals vary.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Tabrisī explain aẓfar for long nails; Jishumī gives the idiom kalīl al-ẓufr. Al-Farrāʾ lists aẓāfīr, aẓāfira, aẓāfir and aẓfār; al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Anbārī, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn record ẓufr, aẓfur/aẓfūr and plural variants, supported by anonymous poetry. Samīn distinguishes regular aẓāfīr from irregular aẓāfir."}, {"id": "6:146/q03/p2", "position": "A hoof can be called a nail figuratively.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites poets calling a hoof a foot and feet hooves, and al-Ḥuṭayʾa's human lips called camel mushāfir; al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Elmalılı report the analogy. Elmalılı compares broad Turkish tırnak."}, {"id": "6:146/q03/p3", "position": "Hooves and talons are literally varieties of nails, differing by size and use.", "reasons": "Al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm says both are soft bone grown from nourishment, can be cut, and serve digging or grasping."}]}
{"id": "6:146/q04", "question": "Which animals are meant by كُلَّ ذِى ظُفُرٍ?", "turns_on": "Whether the defining feature is unsplit toes, literal claws, metaphorical hooves, or a narrower named group.", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q04/p1", "position": "All creatures with unsplit toes or undivided feet, notably camels and ostriches and often geese and ducks.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd, Mujāhid, Qatāda, al-Suddī and others transmit this. Ibn Jurayj adds wild ass and contrasts chickens and sparrows; Qatāda also mentions fish in one report. Some wording calls these cloven-hoofed while examples and distinction mean undivided toes. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān reject camel-only as too narrow. Mujāhid's report also names al-warīna."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p2", "position": "Every clawed bird and every hoofed beast.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Balkhī and others use nail figuratively for hoof, supported by poetry; al-Rāzī and Ālūsī object that it would wrongly include cattle and sheep."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p3", "position": "Every animal or bird with a digit, broadly including camels, predators and birds.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and Bursevī include formerly permitted creatures now barred; al-Biqāʿī emphasizes finger-like claws; Elmalılı favors a broad reading except cattle and sheep and says it excludes fish but includes swine, single-hoofed animals and birds. Ibn ʿĀshūr expressly includes rabbits and hyraxes."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p4", "position": "Camels alone.", "reasons": "Attributed to Ibn Zayd, Abū Zayd, and one report from Ibn ʿAbbās; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān object that this is too narrow."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p5", "position": "Predators or hunting animals with claws and talons, including dogs, cats and birds of prey.", "reasons": "Al-Jubbāʾī and al-Rāzī favor literal claws; al-Rāzī objects that including hoofed cattle and sheep conflicts with their separate treatment. Study Quran sees a carnivore ban."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p6", "position": "Camels and ostriches specifically.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj favors these because ostriches have camel-like nails. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid reports give the pair, sometimes as examples of the wider unsplit category."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p7", "position": "Non-hunting nail-bearing creatures, distinguished from hunters with claws.", "reasons": "Thaʿlab and lexicographers distinguish ẓufr from mikhlab; al-Naqqāsh objects that lions also have nails."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p8", "position": "The rooster and other creatures with separated toes are included.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr gives a contrary report including a rooster; Ibn Kathīr contrasts it with his unsplit-toe definition."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p9", "position": "Clawed birds, hoofed quadrupeds, and fanged predators together.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī gives this three-part animal-kind list."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p10", "position": "Camels, ostriches, and some birds and fish are included.", "reasons": "One Qatāda report adds fish, though another Qatāda report gives the ordinary unsplit-toe list."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p11", "position": "Ostriches and wild asses only.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk is reported thus; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the restriction as too narrow."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p12", "position": "Every clawed animal that had previously been lawful to the Jews.", "reasons": "Ālūsī allows this contextual qualification because some clawed animals were already prohibited before the punitive generalization."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p13", "position": "The pig is additionally included among animals forbidden by this expression.", "reasons": "Ḥanish al-Ṣanʿānī adds it in Ibn Abī Ḥātim's report."}, {"id": "6:146/q04/p14", "position": "Animals with intact hooves, including camels and rabbits, were barred under Jewish law.", "reasons": "Islahi links the term to the Jewish split-hoof and cud-chewing criterion and contrasts Abrahamic permission."}]}
{"id": "6:146/q05", "question": "What did the ban on each clawed animal cover?", "turns_on": "Whether the object is the animal itself or an omitted prey item.", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q05/p1", "position": "The whole animal, including meat and fat, was forbidden to Jews.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān distinguish this from cattle and sheep, whose meat remained lawful. {"id": "6:146/q06", "question": "Are clawed predators and birds forbidden to Muslims by this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the Jewish-specific construction excludes a Prophetic prohibition for Muslims.", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q06/p1", "position": "The verse supports permission for Muslims; a solitary report banning fanged predators and clawed birds cannot override it.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the restriction is exclusive to Jews and supports Mālik; he rejects the reported Prophetic ban as contrary to the Book. {"id": "6:146/q07", "question": "How does وَمِنَ ٱلْبَقَرِ وَٱلْغَنَمِ attach syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether min depends on the following or preceding ḥarramnā, or is an inserted or partitive connector.", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q07/p1", "position": "The fronted phrase attaches to the following حَرَّمْنَا and introduces the fats taken from cattle and sheep.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn answer Abū al-Baqāʾ's objection: a prepositional phrase and object are both complements and can exchange order; a pronoun can require the order, supported by a poetic fronted adverb. {"id": "6:146/q08", "question": "What do the surrounding notes say al-anʿām and bahīma include?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q08/p1", "position": "Al-anʿām includes cattle, sheep, goats and camels; bahīma is wider, and bahīmat al-anʿām can extend to similar edible ruminants.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī calls livestock a subset of living creatures without reason; some linguists include gazelles and wild cattle without fangs."}]}

{"id": "6:146/q12", "question": "May Muslims eat fat or animals that Jews regard as forbidden when Jews slaughter them?", "turns_on": "Whether Jewish intent at slaughter or Islam's later permission controls the food's status.", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q12/p1", "position": "Such fat and slaughter are permitted to Muslims.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī and most scholars say Islam lifted the restriction; Jewish mistaken belief has no legal force. {"id": "6:146/q13", "question": "What do reports say Jews did with forbidden fats?", "turns_on": "The reports' wording and occasion vary.", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q13/p1", "position": "They melted or processed prohibited fats, sold them, and consumed the proceeds; the Prophet condemned or cursed them.", "reasons": "Jābir places a sale prohibition in the Conquest year, covering wine, carrion, pork and idols; the Prophet rejected the suggested uses of carrion fat. ʿUmar cites the Jewish precedent when condemning Samura's wine sale. {"id": "6:146/q14", "question": "What legal rule about selling forbidden food is drawn from these reports?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q14/p1", "position": "When God forbids a food, its sale price is also forbidden.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās explicitly states the principle in the reports; Jābir's Conquest report rejects sale despite practical uses of carrion fat, and ʿUmar applies the precedent to wine."}]}
{"id": "6:146/q15", "question": "What fat is meant by what their backs carry?", "turns_on": "Whether the exception is the attached back layer, includes flank, or specifically means tail fat.", "positions": [{"id": "6:146/q15/p1", "position": "Fat attached to the backs, often extending along the shoulders, sides and flanks, was permitted.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is often cited; al-Kashshāf calls it thin back and flank fat, Muqātil includes shoulders and the sheep's rump, Bursevī extends shoulders to hips inside and out, Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it fat mixed with flesh, and Islahi calls it inseparable from meat."}, {"id": "6:146/q15/p2", "position": "It is the tail or rump fat.", "reasons": "Abū Ṣāliḥ and al-Suddī identify tail fat with the back-carried exception; Ibn Qutayba calls it al-aliyya. {"id": "7:24/q07", "question": "Where did Iblis land?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted sites; Ibn Kathir treats location reports as uncertain Israelite material.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q07/p1", "position": "He landed in the Maysan or Basra area.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan specifies Dast Maysan near Basra; Ibn Atiyya reports Maysan or Basra and quotes Ibn Umar saying Iblis spread his rich carpet there. {"id": "7:24/q08", "question": "Where did the serpent land?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q08/p1", "position": "The serpent landed in Isfahan.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan and later reports concur, though Ibn Kathir doubts landing place reports as a class."}]}

{"id": "7:24/q10", "question": "What happened to Adam when he descended and began earthly life?", "turns_on": "These are distinct transmitted details of Adam's descent, not exclusive accounts.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q10/p1", "position": "Adam descended bowed, learned labor, and had to cultivate and prepare his own food.", "reasons": "Raja ibn Abi Salama describes Adam's hands on his knees and head bowed, contrasting Iblis's interlocked fingers and raised head. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report ironworking and farming, followed by plowing, watering, harvesting, threshing, winnowing, kneading, baking and cooking. {"id": "7:24/q13", "question": "What does the enmity describe, and between whom?", "turns_on": "The range of the mutual pronouns and whether the serpent or human descendants are included.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q13/p1", "position": "Adam or humanity and Iblis are opposed to each other.", "reasons": "Muqatil says Iblis is enemy to Adam and Eve and they to him. Al-Nasafi takes the hostility as reciprocal. Ibn Kathir cites 20:123 for the central Adam–Iblis conflict. Bursevi says Iblis resents Adam's succession and his own lost leadership; his hostility is innate like a scorpion's sting or wolf's theft, while humans must oppose their father's enemy. Al-Tabataba'i sees antagonism in their different natures; Islahi says Satan seeks to mislead Adam's offspring while they can defeat his designs and regain Paradise."}, {"id": "7:24/q13/p2", "position": "The hostility extends to the descendants of Adam and Iblis and also includes conflicts among humans.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i names both sets of offspring and interhuman enmity. {"id": "7:24/q14", "question": "How does the enmity clause work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is dependent as a circumstance or independent as a new statement.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q14/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause describing their state on descent.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi parse it as a hal; al-Alusi allows simultaneous or prospective circumstance."}, {"id": "7:24/q14/p2", "position": "It is a fresh sentence answering what their descent will be like.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this grammatical analysis from some grammarians."}]}
